overview: Dvaravati names connected towns, Buddhist artistic traditions and early polities in what is now Thailand. It should not be treated as one securely bounded empire. The map’s 600 to 1100 span is approximate; its changing southern extensions do not prove unified rule over the peninsula, and some sites discussed here lie beyond its shaded area.

periods.title: Urban and religious networks
periods.summary: Towns, inscriptions and monumental art developed through local changes and long-distance connections.

periods.title: Changing regional powers
periods.summary: Khmer influence increased unevenly. The map endpoint does not mark simultaneous abandonment of Dvaravati towns.

items.text: Dvaravati’s impressive towns did not appear from nowhere in 600. Archaeologist Stephen Murphy argues for earlier development, especially in the fourth and fifth centuries, based on excavated pottery and settlement sequences. Communities adapted imported ideas over time, and scholars still debate how many rulers controlled the later network.

U Thong had an oval plan surrounded by a waterway and an earthen embankment. Its museum records at least twenty ancient monuments within and around the city. Looking at the town as a whole reveals an organized landscape of settlement and religious buildings, rather than just a collection of beautiful statues.

At Si Thep, moats enclosed an Inner Town and an Outer Town. Nearby stood the huge Khao Klang Nok monument and the Khao Thamorrat cave monastery. These remains preserve both Buddhist and Hindu traditions. Different sacred places formed part of the same regional landscape, while local sculptors developed recognizable ways of depicting bodies and movement.

A silver medallion found near Wat Phra Paton in Nakhon Pathom in 1943 carries “śrīdvāravatīśvarapuṇya”, translated “meritorious deed of the ruler of Dvāravatī”. This is a scholarly Roman-letter transliteration of Sanskrit, not a reproduction of the ancient script. The seventh- or eighth-century object, only 1.7 centimeters across, provides written evidence for the name Dvaravati and a ruler’s religious patronage.

Inscriptions from central and northeastern Thailand used several languages: Mon and Khmer for donations or dedications, and Pali or Sanskrit for religious quotations. Written Mon is important evidence, but it does not tell us that every household spoke the same language. The surviving texts record selected activities and people.

Dvaravati stone Wheels of the Law could stand above viewers on tall pillars. A separate stone block joined the pillar and wheel; surviving pieces show no metal pins securing the assembly. Scholars infer that weight held it together. Stone deer found at Dvaravati sites are interpreted as companions to the wheels, recalling the deer park where the Buddha first taught.

Making a sacred image could itself be a religious action. Between the seventh and ninth centuries, craftspeople produced clay plaques showing episodes from the Buddha’s life. Images were stamped into clay, allowing a mold to repeat a design. The act of making these images was understood as earning religious merit, connecting manual work with devotion.

At Phromtin Tai, ancient plant remains show rice becoming dominant by the Iron Age and Dvaravati phases. A study of this area found continued reliance on rain-fed cultivation, rather than evidence for intensified plowing and irrigation. This is a regional result: Dvaravati farmers worked in different landscapes, so one field system cannot explain every town’s food supply.

At Dong Mae Nang Muang, a settlement occupied roughly from the eighth to twelfth centuries, grinding stones and spindle whorls reveal food preparation and textile work. Small terracotta oil lamps could light homes or sacred buildings. Before a piece of clothing reached someone’s shoulders, thread had to be made by hand.

Dong Mae Nang Muang also yielded everyday dishes, bowls, jars and round-bodied pots. Turquoise-glazed pottery identified as Persian ware, around the ninth century, points to exchange reaching far inland from coastal trading towns. An attractive pot could travel through several hands; finding it does not establish the nationality of the family that used it.

A small terracotta figure displayed at the Somdet Phra Narai National Museum shows a seated woman holding a child, apparently feeding it. The museum considers several possibilities: a mother, a caregiver or the Buddhist child-protecting figure Hariti. Dated broadly to Dvaravati times, it brings care for children into view, although its exact identity and use remain uncertain.

A gold ear ornament found during construction in the U Thong museum grounds in 2010 consists of two hinged halves. Related ornaments appear on a terracotta relief of musicians from Khu Bua. Comparing jewelry with pictures of people wearing it helps explain how unfamiliar objects worked. The tiny hinge made this ornament an engineering project as well as decoration.

Excavations at U Thong studied by San Thaiyanonda identified glass-bead and metal working in the tenth and eleventh centuries. The researcher suggests some products may have been exported through connections with southern ports. These were places where people made goods as well as received them, giving craftspeople a role in the town’s wider trading life.

At Phu Hang Nak, west of U Thong, some visitors had interpreted stone remains as prehistoric monuments. Fine Arts Department excavations instead found Dvaravati buildings and artifacts, including evidence around the ninth century, with sparse later reuse. Digging beneath the surface changed the story: an impressive-looking pile of stones does not date itself.

Dong Mae Nang Muang’s inscription K966 dates to 1167, after this map record ends. Its Khmer and Pali text and royal titles suggest Khmer influence. Yet the excavators found no sharp change in the town’s material culture or new Khmer religious monuments. They interpret this as evidence that much of the existing population remained.

ending.text: Dvaravati traditions changed at different speeds. Khmer influence grew from about the tenth century, and Suryavarman II invaded central Thailand in the first half of the twelfth. These political changes did not erase every town or its Buddhist practices. The map’s 1100 cutoff is not a documented, simultaneous fall of one empire.
